paragraphs: When a language model is uncertain, refusing to answer can discard useful information, while adding words of uncertainty can make an answer difficult to use. This paper studies how to preserve useful content while adjusting how specific a response is. Its central proposal is Conformal Linguistic Calibration, or CLC.

CLC treats linguistic calibration as predicting a set of possible answers. This connects the wording of an uncertain response to the range of answers it allows. The framework uses linguistic pragmatics to connect this view with abstention, placing both within a shared account of how models communicate uncertainty. Its implementation lets users control response imprecision.

The reported results show calibrated outputs with conformal guarantees on factual accuracy. The approach also supports fine-tuning models to rewrite claims according to uncertainty. The contribution is a way to manage the tradeoff between detail and factual reliability: responses can become less specific when uncertainty warrants it, while still conveying information.
neurips-2025-conformal-linguistic-calibr.tldr: CLC turns uncertainty-aware wording into answer set prediction, enabling controlled specificity with conformal guarantees on factual accuracy.

paragraphs: Counterfactual inference asks how an outcome would differ under a change to the system that produced it. This paper studies that question for structural causal models containing cycles. Its motivation is that many real systems, including biological systems, have feedback loops, whereas most counterfactual frameworks traditionally assume an acyclic structure.

The distinction matters because an acyclic graph rules out a chain of dependencies that returns to its starting point. A cyclic model allows that feedback structure. The paper therefore places counterfactual questions in a setting where dependencies need not follow a one-way ordering, bringing the modeling setup closer to the feedback systems highlighted in the abstract.

Within this setting, the work considers shift–scale interventions: soft, policy-style changes that shift or rescale a variable’s mechanism, or do both. The stated contribution is the study of counterfactual inference under this combination of cyclic dependencies and mechanism adjustments. It broadens the problem setting beyond acyclic models to examine changes within systems that contain feedback.
neurips-2025-cyclic-counterfactuals-unde.tldr: The paper studies counterfactual inference in causal systems with feedback loops under interventions that shift or rescale variable mechanisms.

paragraphs: Combining photographs from different viewpoints becomes difficult when objects lie at substantially different depths. The resulting parallax can leave objects misaligned or produce ghosting in the stitched image. This paper introduces a stitching method that uses depth consistency to address alignment and blending together.

The alignment stage combines multiple processing stages with global depth regularization. Its purpose is to improve agreement between views of the same target across different depth ranges. During fusion, a graph-based computation finds a low-cost stitching seam. The method then spreads this seam into a soft transition region, locating where the images should blend to reduce visible effects of remaining alignment errors.

The method also incorporates reparameterization to reduce computational overhead in shift regression, improving efficiency while maintaining performance. Experiments report superior results against existing methods. The approach matters because it addresses both where corresponding image content should align and how views should merge, while also treating computational cost as part of the stitching design.
neurips-2025-depth-supervised-fusion-net.tldr: Depth-constrained alignment and soft seam fusion improve image stitching under parallax, with reparameterization reducing computational overhead.

paragraphs: Learned simulators operating on mesh graphs can struggle with effects that span a whole structure, such as bending. Local message passing makes these relationships difficult to capture, while repeated next-step predictions can accumulate errors. ROBIN addresses these problems by combining a hierarchical graph network with diffusion-based refinement.

Its graph hierarchy uses algebraic multigrid coarsening to pass information across multiple mesh resolutions. This lets the model represent both local dynamics and broader structural effects, including those involved in bending and contact. Its inference scheme overlaps denoising work across a window of physical time steps, sharing the cost of refinement across the simulated sequence.

The authors evaluate ROBIN on two- and three-dimensional solid mechanics problems with geometric, material, and contact nonlinearities. It achieves the best reported accuracy on all evaluated tasks, outperforming existing next-step learned simulators. Inference is up to an order of magnitude faster than standard diffusion simulators. These findings support combining multiscale information exchange with temporally overlapping refinement for accurate, more efficient learned simulation.
neurips-2025-diffusion-based-hierarchica.tldr: ROBIN combines multiscale graph processing with overlapping diffusion refinement to improve nonlinear solid simulation accuracy and inference speed.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that claims about privacy in human pose estimation need measurable evidence. Systems in this field are still evaluated mainly through accuracy, even as privacy concerns receive more attention. The authors contend that describing a system as privacy-preserving or human-centric requires privacy itself to be assessed.

Their critique extends beyond the pose estimator to how systems are deployed. Transmitting and storing data can introduce additional risks, and continued reliance on RGB inputs remains a concern. They also identify a gap between privacy claims and evaluation practice: privacy is not defined in measurable terms or connected to regulatory requirements, and existing benchmarks do not adequately reflect legal and ethical constraints.

The proposed shift is to make privacy part of system design, testing, and comparison. This is an argument for changing what counts as evidence of a good pose estimation system. Accuracy measurements address prediction quality; the paper calls for privacy evaluation to become an explicit part of assessing the system as well.
neurips-2025-dont-call-it-privacy-preser.tldr: This position paper argues that human pose estimation needs measurable privacy evaluation to substantiate privacy-preserving and human-centric claims.

paragraphs: FACT addresses inconsistent hallucinations in language models: outputs that undermine reliable reasoning about facts. Existing approaches often depend on training tailored to particular tasks or focus mainly on numerical reasoning. The paper seeks a more general training approach that can benefit natural language tasks beyond those specific settings.

The method starts from the observation that factual text contains patterns that can be represented through programming structures. Training alternates between converting text into code and converting code into text. By placing these representations in a shared semantic space, FACT aims to transfer the structural rigor and logical consistency of programming languages into natural language outputs.

Using a small subset of Wiki-40B-en, the authors evaluate FACT on three leading language models and four datasets covering question answering and summarization. They report reductions in inconsistent hallucinations of 2.7%–8.0% and overall performance improvements of 2.5%–6.1%. These results support alternating code–text training as a task-agnostic way to improve factual consistency across the evaluated language tasks.
neurips-2025-fact-mitigating-inconsisten.tldr: FACT alternates text-to-code and code-to-text training to reduce inconsistent hallucinations and improve question answering and summarization.

paragraphs: FGBench examines whether language models can reason about molecular properties using information about functional groups within molecules. Many existing datasets focus on properties of whole molecules, leaving these finer structural relationships underrepresented. The paper introduces data intended to connect localized molecular structure with textual reasoning.

The dataset contains 625,000 reasoning problems covering 245 functional groups. Groups are annotated and located within each molecule, supporting interoperability and further multimodal use. Problems include regression and classification, organized around the effects of a single group, interactions among multiple groups, and direct comparisons between molecules. This organization makes functional-group information central to the reasoning task.

Evaluation on 7,000 curated examples indicates that current leading language models struggle with this level of property reasoning. The findings identify a gap in their ability to connect fine-grained structure with molecular properties. The authors propose the dataset construction methodology as a foundation for further question–answer generation, with the potential to support more interpretable, structure-aware models for chemistry.
neurips-2025-fgbench-a-dataset-and-bench.tldr: FGBench provides 625,000 functional-group reasoning problems and finds that current language models struggle with fine-grained molecular property reasoning.

paragraphs: Diffusion policies offer exploration capabilities and can represent multiple action possibilities, but incorporating them into on-policy reinforcement learning presents a technical obstacle. Algorithms such as PPO need action log-likelihoods, which are difficult to compute for the generative policies discussed here. GenPO targets this barrier in settings suited to large-scale parallel simulation.

The framework uses exact diffusion inversion to create invertible action mappings. A doubled dummy action mechanism alternates updates to enable this invertibility, making the required likelihood computation possible. The resulting action log-likelihoods also support unbiased estimates of entropy and KL divergence, allowing entropy regularization and learning rates that adapt according to KL divergence.

Experiments across eight IsaacLab benchmarks report better performance than the evaluated reinforcement learning baselines. Tasks span legged locomotion, dexterous manipulation, aerial control, and robotic arms. The contribution is a route for bringing diffusion policies into on-policy training frameworks, connecting their expressive action generation with the parallelized training infrastructure used for these robotic tasks.
neurips-2025-genpo-generative-diffusion-.tldr: GenPO makes diffusion policy likelihoods computable through invertible action mappings, enabling on-policy reinforcement learning with strong simulated robotics results.

paragraphs: MIX-HIC aims to build a more integrated representation of 3D genome information. Although deep learning has improved individual analytical tasks in this area, the paper identifies a broader gap in combining different forms of genomic knowledge. Its foundation model brings 3D genome structure and epigenomic tracks into a shared representation.

The architecture includes cross-modal interaction and mapping blocks to combine these heterogeneous inputs. Their role is to align and aggregate information across the two modalities so that the resulting representation captures knowledge from both. The authors also introduce a pretraining dataset containing more than one million paired examples of Hi-C contact maps and epigenomic tracks.

Experiments report significant improvements over existing leading methods across diverse downstream tasks. These results support multimodal pretraining as a way to develop representations useful beyond a single 3D genomics analysis. The paired dataset is also part of the contribution, providing a large-scale resource for learning connections between these inputs and exploring their functional implications.
neurips-2025-multimodal-3d-genome-pre-tr.tldr: MIX-HIC jointly pretrains on 3D genome structure and epigenomic tracks, improving performance across the evaluated downstream genomics tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions made under a limited resource budget when reward and cost distributions can change adversarially. It covers both allocation problems where rewards and costs are visible before choosing an action and learning problems where they become available afterward. In the latter setting, feedback may be full or bandit.

Arbitrary changes make sublinear regret impossible in the unrestricted setting. The authors introduce guidance through a spending plan that specifies expected resource use across rounds. Their primal–dual methods achieve sublinear regret relative to baselines that follow that plan. The comparator restriction is central: the guarantee depends on which resource-use patterns the competing baseline follows.

Performance improves when the plan distributes the budget in a well-balanced way across rounds. The paper also provides a robust variant for highly imbalanced plans and studies comparisons against benchmarks that depart from the prescribed plan. Together, these results clarify how guidance about spending can support learning guarantees despite adversarial changes in rewards and costs.
neurips-2025-no-regret-learning-under-ad.tldr: A spending plan enables sublinear regret against plan-following baselines under adversarially changing rewards and resource costs.

paragraphs: Classical image filters use normalization to keep their responses consistent and avoid unwanted visual effects. Learned convolutional filters usually lack comparable constraints, even when they resemble familiar edge or blob detectors. This paper argues that this omission distorts filter responses when images undergo atmospheric transfer, contributing to incorrect model outputs.

The proposed modification normalizes filters and then applies learnable scaling and shifting, in a pattern analogous to batch normalization. The authors state that this makes the filters atmosphere-equivariant: their responses respect the relevant transformation relationship. The method applies to convolutional networks and vision transformers that depend on convolution, bringing a classical filtering principle into learned vision architectures.

Experiments show significant gains on benchmarks involving artificial and natural intensity variation. The authors also report a setting where their ResNet34 substantially outperforms CLIP. Their analysis links unnormalized filters to degraded performance and finds that normalization regularizes learning, encourages filter diversity, and improves robustness and generalization in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-normalize-filters-classical.tldr: Normalizing learned image filters improves robustness to intensity variation by incorporating consistency principles from classical image processing.

paragraphs: This paper asks when a densely connected community can be detected inside a bipartite graph. Under the no-community hypothesis, every possible edge has probability p0. Under the alternative, an unknown subgraph has a higher edge probability, p0 plus a positive increase, while the remaining edges retain the background probability.

The main goal is to characterize how large that increase must be for a test to keep both false alarms and missed detections sufficiently small. The authors derive non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds on this detection threshold. These bounds match across all configurations of the two graph dimensions and the two community dimensions considered in the model.

For sufficiently dense graphs, the paper also constructs minimax-optimal tests that reach the fundamental detection limits. The tests combine hard-thresholded nonlinear statistics of the adjacency matrix. The contribution therefore connects an information-theoretic question about detectability with concrete statistical tests, while retaining the stated density condition for the optimality result.
neurips-2025-optimal-community-detection.tldr: The paper characterizes matching detection thresholds for bipartite communities and develops optimal tests when the graph is sufficiently dense.

paragraphs: Mobile manipulators must connect high-level instructions with navigation and physical actions. Open-world tasks add difficulty because instructions and environments can vary, and decisions need to reflect both the broader scene and the robot’s current state. OWMM-Agent addresses this integration problem through a multimodal agent architecture.

The agent maintains scene frames from multiple viewpoints alongside robot state information and controls the robot through function calls. To address hallucinations associated with domain shift, the authors add an agentic data synthesis pipeline and use its output for instruction fine-tuning. The resulting OWMM-VLM combines global scene understanding, state tracking, and multimodal action generation within one model.

Experiments report leading performance relative to the foundation models evaluated, including GPT-4o, together with strong zero-shot generalization in real-world settings. The approach matters because it combines architectural support for ongoing scene and state awareness with training adapted to mobile manipulation. Both parts address the challenge of translating open-ended instructions into actions grounded in the robot’s situation.
neurips-2025-owmm-agent-open-world-mobil.tldr: OWMM-Agent combines multiview scene and robot state tracking with synthesized training data to improve open-world mobile manipulation.

paragraphs: Video enhancement models use information from multiple frames to improve video quality, but Transformer-based approaches can be expensive to run on edge devices. Reducing numerical precision offers efficiency benefits, yet existing quantization methods can lose fine details. PMQ-VE addresses how to preserve enhancement quality when weights and activations use fewer bits.

The framework has two stages. Backtracking-based Multi-Frame Quantization initializes clipping bounds using percentiles, then refines them through iterative search with pruning and backtracking. This addresses the need to adapt representational capacity across frames. Progressive Multi-Teacher Distillation then trains low-bit models using both full-precision teachers and multiple higher-bit integer teachers, reducing dependence on a full-precision teacher alone.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across several tasks and benchmarks relative to the evaluated alternatives. The approach treats low-bit enhancement as both a numerical range selection problem and a training problem. Its two stages aim to retain the temporal information and fine details that can be damaged when quantization is applied directly.
neurips-2025-pmq-ve-progressive-multi-fr.tldr: PMQ-VE combines frame-aware quantization search with progressive multi-teacher training to improve low-bit video enhancement quality.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning builds a policy from an existing dataset without collecting additional interactions. Learning effectively often requires substantial, diverse data to reduce uncertainty, but gathering that data can be costly or infeasible. This paper proposes pretraining a Q-network’s feature representation to make better use of limited offline data.

The method uses a shared backbone in two stages. First, a transition prediction head trains the backbone to represent information useful for predicting transitions. Second, the backbone is combined with a Q-value head and trained using an offline reinforcement learning objective. The framework is designed as a plug-and-play initialization compatible with any such objective.

Experiments on D4RL, Robomimic, V-D4RL, and ExoRL report substantial improvements in performance and data efficiency across diverse domains. The authors also report that using only 10% of the dataset can outperform standard offline reinforcement learning baselines trained on the full data. These findings support transition-focused representation pretraining as a useful preparation step for learning values from limited experience.
neurips-2025-pretraining-a-shared-q-netw.tldr: Pretraining a shared Q-network backbone on transition prediction improves offline reinforcement learning performance and data efficiency.

paragraphs: Differential privacy research often starts with a fixed privacy budget and asks what utility it permits. Practitioners may instead have a target utility and want to determine the privacy cost of reaching it. This paper develops theoretical tools for that utility-first perspective using ex-post privacy guarantees.

Earlier results showed how progressively reducing correlated noise could produce increasingly accurate estimates, with privacy cost attributed to the least noisy released estimate. Those results largely concerned simple Laplace or Gaussian mechanisms. This work generalizes the approach to any sequence of private estimators, with at most a doubling of the original privacy budget.

The authors further show that hyperparameter tuning for these estimators, including choosing an optimal privacy budget, can be performed without additional privacy cost within their framework. They also extend the results to ex-post Rényi differential privacy. The contribution broadens the types of estimators that utility-first privacy analysis can support and incorporates tuning into the accounting, rather than limiting the analysis to simple noise mechanisms.
neurips-2025-private-hyperparameter-tuni.tldr: The paper generalizes utility-first privacy guarantees to arbitrary sequences of private estimators and supports tuning without additional privacy cost.

paragraphs: This paper probes language models by deleting layers or swapping adjacent layers during inference. Without fine-tuning afterward, the tested models retain 72–95% of their original top-1 prediction accuracy. Sensitivity varies by depth: changing early or final layers causes the largest degradation, while removing middle layers is comparatively well tolerated.

The authors use this pattern to motivate a four-stage hypothesis of inference. First, local context transforms raw token embeddings into higher-level representations. Next, the model refines features relevant to tasks and entities. A third stage aggregates hidden states into plausible next-token predictions, and a final calibration stage suppresses irrelevant features to finalize the output distribution.

The proposed stages synthesize behavioral and mechanistic evidence across different model families and sizes. They offer an interpretation of why interventions have different effects at different depths. The four-stage account remains a hypothesis about depth-dependent computation; the empirical result is that substantial structural interventions can preserve much of the measured prediction accuracy.
neurips-2025-remarkable-robustness-of-ll.tldr: Layer deletion and swapping reveal uneven sensitivity across language model depth, motivating a four-stage hypothesis of inference.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts language models route computation through selected expert modules. SAFEx investigates a safety risk associated with this structure: aligned behavior may depend heavily on particular experts. The paper calls this positional vulnerability and develops a stability-based procedure for identifying and validating experts important to safety.

The framework distinguishes experts involved in detecting harmful user content from experts involved in controlling the model’s response. Targeted interventions test the causal role of the selected modules. In Qwen3-30B-A3B, which has 6,144 experts across its MoE layers, disabling 12 selected experts reduces the refusal rate by 22%. This provides evidence of concentrated safety behavior in that model.

The authors also test lightweight LoRA adaptation across different expert groups and compose the updates using negative weight merging targeted at response-control experts. This improves refusal under adversarial prompts without retraining the full model. The results connect a diagnosis of concentrated safety dependence with expert-level interventions intended to strengthen safety behavior in routed architectures.
neurips-2025-safex-analyzing-vulnerabili.tldr: SAFEx identifies concentrated safety roles in MoE experts and tests targeted interventions that expose vulnerabilities and improve adversarial refusal.

paragraphs: Schrödinger bridges provide a dynamic formulation of entropy-regularized optimal transport between distributions. Recent flow-based methods make these problems more scalable, including Iterative Markovian Fitting, which solves them through repeated bridge-matching steps. This paper extends that procedure from the usual setting to costs connecting several distributions through a tree.

The tree structure matters because it organizes a multi-marginal transport problem: the objective involves several distributions rather than a single pair. Wasserstein barycentres arise as a special case of this formulation. Extending bridge matching to trees therefore makes the method applicable to a broader family of distribution-matching problems within a common algorithmic framework.

The resulting algorithm retains the advantages attributed to Iterative Markovian Fitting over Iterative Proportional Fitting in this tree-based setting. For Wasserstein barycentres, it can be understood as extending a widely used fixed-point approach to work with flow-based entropic transport solvers. Each iteration still requires only simple bridge-matching steps, connecting the broader formulation to a practical repeated operation.
neurips-2025-schrodinger-bridge-matching.tldr: The paper extends iterative Schrödinger bridge matching to tree-structured transport problems, including entropic Wasserstein barycentres.

paragraphs: ShotBench evaluates whether vision-language models understand the visual language of filmmaking. Strong general visual reasoning does not by itself establish this specialized ability. The benchmark focuses evaluation on cinematic understanding, using material annotated by trained annotators or curated from professional cinematography resources.

It contains 3,049 still images and 500 clips from more than 200 films, with 3,608 question–answer pairs spanning eight cinematography dimensions. Evaluation of more than 20 leading models reveals limitations in fine-grained perception and cinematic reasoning. These results make the benchmark useful for distinguishing broad visual competence from the more specific understanding required to interpret movie shots.

The authors also create ShotQA, a training dataset of approximately 70,000 question–answer pairs, and train ShotVL through supervised fine-tuning followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization. ShotVL surpasses all open-source and proprietary models evaluated on ShotBench. The work therefore contributes both a specialized assessment and a training approach that substantially improves performance on that assessment.
neurips-2025-shotbench-expert-level-cine.tldr: ShotBench exposes gaps in cinematic understanding, while the authors’ ShotVL model outperforms all evaluated competitors on the benchmark.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a frozen video generator trained to predict future frames can reveal optical flow without flow-specific fine-tuning. The motivation is that labeled flow data is scarce and synthetic data can differ from real video. The approach probes a model’s predictions by making a small localized change to its input.

The authors find that successful extraction is aided by distributional future-frame prediction, independently represented spatiotemporal patches, and decoding that can condition on arbitrary subsets of future pixels. These properties occur together in the LRAS architecture. Their KL-tracing procedure perturbs the first frame, predicts one step ahead, and measures divergence between the perturbed and unperturbed predictive distributions.

Without flow-specific fine-tuning, the method is competitive with leading task-specific models on TAP-Vid DAVIS and TAP-Vid Kubric, covering real and synthetic video. The findings support counterfactual prompting as an effective way to extract motion information from controllable generative models. They also identify architectural properties that help this form of inference work.
neurips-2025-taming-generative-video-mod.tldr: KL-tracing extracts competitive optical flow from a frozen video generator by measuring how localized input perturbations change predicted distributions.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can produce self-reflection that does not reliably check whether their answers are correct. RISE addresses this by training problem solving and self-verification together within one online reinforcement learning process. The goal is to make checking a learned capability alongside solution generation.

During each iteration, the model first produces solutions and then critiques those same solutions generated under its current policy. An outcome verifier provides verifiable rewards for both activities, and both trajectories contribute to the policy update. This connects verification training to the model’s own current behavior, allowing feedback on both its answers and its assessment of those answers.

Across mathematical reasoning benchmarks, RISE consistently improves problem-solving accuracy while strengthening self-verification. The authors also find benefits from online verification and additional verification computation. Trained models check their reasoning more frequently and more accurately. These results support explicitly rewarding verification within reasoning training as a way to make self-checking more dependable in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2025-trust-but-verify-a-self-ver.tldr: RISE jointly rewards solution generation and self-verification, improving mathematical reasoning accuracy and the reliability of models’ self-checks.

paragraphs: Learning becomes difficult when a dataset combines incorrect labels with strongly uneven class frequencies. Label correction methods rely on relatively unbiased predictions to recover the true distribution, while methods for class imbalance need that distribution to correct prediction bias. Unlocker identifies this circular dependence as a reason straightforward combinations can fail.

The proposed framework separates the problem into two linked optimization levels. The inner level trains the model using noisy-label learning, incorporating long-tail methods to select and correct labels more fairly. The outer level adapts the adjustment strength so that correcting imbalance does not push predictions too far or leave too much bias.

The authors prove convergence of their bilevel formulation by transforming the outer objective into an equivalent problem with a closed-form solution. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show effectiveness in reducing bias and handling long-tailed noisy labels. The contribution is a coordinated way to update label handling and bias adjustment when each depends on information the other is trying to improve.
neurips-2025-unlocker-disentangle-the-de.tldr: Unlocker uses bilevel optimization to coordinate noisy-label correction and class-imbalance adjustment, addressing their circular dependence.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can spend many tokens on unnecessary reflection, raising inference costs. VeriThinker aims to shorten these reasoning chains by fine-tuning solely on an auxiliary verification task. The model learns to judge the correctness of chain-of-thought solutions, rather than being trained directly on concise solutions to the original task.

The proposed mechanism is that better verification helps a model recognize whether further reflection is necessary. Experiments show substantially shorter reasoning while maintaining or slightly improving accuracy. This makes verification training relevant to efficiency as well as correctness: learning to assess a solution can reduce the amount of additional reasoning the model produces.

For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on MATH500, reasoning tokens fall from 3,790 to 2,125 while accuracy rises from 94.0% to 94.8%. On AIME25, tokens decrease from 14,321 to 10,287 and accuracy increases from 38.7% to 40.8%. The authors also report zero-shot transfer to speculative reasoning. These results support verification as an indirect route to compressing reasoning in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-verithinker-learning-to-ver.tldr: VeriThinker trains models to verify solutions, reducing reasoning length while preserving or slightly improving accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Signal Temporal Logic can describe robotic tasks with requirements about behavior over time. Turning those requirements into executable trajectories is difficult because the specification must be compatible with the system’s dynamics. This paper studies planning when those dynamics are unknown, using task-agnostic trajectory data for offline training.

The framework separates planning into three parts. It first decomposes the specification into progress requirements and timing constraints. It then searches for timed waypoints satisfying those requirements. Finally, a pretrained diffusion model generates trajectory segments, which are stitched together into a complete plan. This hierarchy connects high-level temporal requirements with trajectory generation learned from data.

The authors formally prove STL satisfaction for their method and report simulation results showing dynamically feasible trajectories across diverse long-horizon tasks. The framework supports zero-shot generalization to new STL tasks without task-specific offline training. Its contribution is to combine reusable trajectory generation with specification-driven waypoint planning, addressing both temporal task structure and the need for executable motion.
neurips-2025-zero-shot-trajectory-planni.tldr: A hierarchical planner combines timed waypoints with pretrained diffusion trajectories to handle new temporal-logic tasks for systems with unknown dynamics.
